extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary criticism / creative writers interested in 19th-century literary values
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-form set of evaluative reflections on authors, poetry, and art (Carlyle, Hegel, Emerson, Longfellow, Bryant, Whittier, Millet) that articulate qualities, strengths, and failings valued in creative writing and art. Useful as a source of implicit criteria for judging prose, poetry, and pictorial art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (the verteber of genius)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential backbone of genius is power — a work's force or commanding quality that shakes comfortable reading circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman: 'the verteber of genius, namely power.' Value is not merely 'maker of books' but that which launches a rasping, questioning, dislocating agitation and shock. Example: Carlyle's power is his final value because he 'shakes our comfortable reading circles.' Works should possess this kind of centripetal force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy as revelation, not mere prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: True 'prophecy' in literature means pouring forth inner, divine spontaneities that reveal truths, not simply forecasting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarification: 'The word prophecy is much misused; it seems narrow'd to prediction merely. ... it means one whose mind bubbles up and pours forth as a fountain, from inner, divine spontaneities revealing God.' Evaluate writing for its revelatory, generative insight rather than only its predictive accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity combined with towering strength
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic of apparent frailty or simplicity that conceals great, enduring strength and stamina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase: 'the simplicity and amid ostensible frailty the towering strength of this man.' Valued voice: unpretentious outward manner but inner durability — an 'old farmer dress'd in brown clothes' whose foibles are fascinating. Look for humble form with powerful substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasping, questioning, dislocating agitation (socially provocative writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing that provokes, agitates, questions social complacency, and dislocates comfortable assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman: not for mere literary merit but 'as launching into the self-complacent atmosphere of our days a rasping, questioning, dislocating agitation and shock.' Such work's value lies in its ability to unsettle and probe public habits and beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, earnest convictions; refusal to temporize
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncompromising moral earnestness and independence of mind; lack of flunkeyism or opportunistic flatteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted judgement: 'Never were convictions more earnest and genuine. Never was there less of a flunkey or temporizer.' Reward writers who risk unpopularity for honesty; penalize flatterers and timid compromisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosing social ills — literature as moral physician/protest
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's role can be to diagnose and protest societal maladies — to provide indignation and exposure of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman: Carlyle is 'by far the most indignant comment or protest anent the fruits of feudalism to-day.' Value works that identify and morally indict social structures (poverty, inequality, degradation). This is a substantive criterion for political/social literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding in real-world observation, not mere bookishness
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for writers who confront facts directly — face-to-face encounters with lived realities — over those who live mainly in books and reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning about Carlyle: 'there was no one in Scotland who had glean'd so much and seen so little.' Evaluate whether the writer's claims and portrayals emerge from tangible observation and experience rather than purely abstract reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal force / celebration of commanding personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: High regard for writing that recognizes or exalts strong, commanding individual personalities — 'born to command' figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman notes Carlyle's admiration for great personalities: 'the great masses of humanity stand for nothing... only the big planets and shining suns for him.' As a criterion, consider how a work treats leadership, heroism, and charismatic figures: sympathetically, critically, or reductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soul-sight / intuitive moral insight beyond argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's capacity for an immediate, non-argumentative apprehension of an underlying moral or cosmic balance — an intuitive 'soul-sight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'a wondrous something... an intuition of the absolute balance... a soul-sight of that divine clue and unseen thread.' Evaluate depth of insight that feels like a root-centre for the mind — intuition that supplements or overrides mere formal reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic coherence and ensemblist unity (Hegelian standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theesthetic and intellectual value in unifying diverse facts, contradictions, and perspectives into a coherent, teleological whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman recounts Hegel: 'the whole earth... are all... necessary sides and unfoldings... held together by central and never-broken unity.' Works that synthesize apparent contradictions into a larger, morally intelligible system score highly on this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about prescriptive remedies; avoid cure-all prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism toward authors who claim a single specific remedy for complex social ills; caution against prescriptive dogmatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman critiques Carlyle's tendency to believe he 'had a clue to the medication of the world's ills' and warns the critic not to 'prescribe a specific for indispensable evils.' Evaluate whether proposals are nuanced and modest rather than absolutist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of dissent and learning from unlikeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Art and criticism teach best when they present sincere opposition; deep lessons are learned from unlikeness and adversaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman: 'we surely learn deepest from unlikeness, from a sincere opponent.' As an evaluative principle, grant merit to works that function as productive counterpoints, provoking rethinking rather than mere agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality and philosophic melody in poetry (Emerson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry valued for sweet, vital melody and the fusion of lyrical quality with philosophical depth ('rhym'd philosophy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson praised: 'sweet, vital-tasting melody, rhym'd philosophy, and poems as amber-clear as the honey of the wild bee.' Assess poems for musical line, tonal clarity, and integration of thought and song.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rich color and graceful narrative/incident (Longfellow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic/poetic-prose strength in the use of vivid color, graceful formal shapes, and well-crafted incidents that render life beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longfellow commended for 'rich color, graceful forms and incidents.' Evaluate descriptive richness, compositional elegance, and the ability to make commonplace events feel refined and significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-air imagery and threnodic sensibility (Bryant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems that pulse with natural imagery — rivers, woods, scents of hayfields — and a recurring elegiac (threnody) tone that touches universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bryant called 'bard of the river and the wood,' 'pulsing the first interior verse-throbs of a mighty world' with threnodies and nature-sense. Score work for sensory, outdoor imagery and a sincere elegiac register when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral energy, zeal, rectitude and the utility of narrowness (Whittier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry valued for fervent moral purpose, rectitude, and zeal — even when accompanied by a certain willful narrowness that preserves moral clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman: Whittier 'lives the zeal, the moral energy... the splendid rectitude and ardor of Luther,' but also 'the wilfulness and narrowness.' Evaluate the moral intensity and integrity of voice, and recognize that some narrowness can be a strength rather than a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impalpable ethical purpose of art (Millet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great visual art (and by extension writing) can embody an unconscious, impalpable ethical purpose that penetrates the viewer/reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Millet: 'then it seem'd to me, with that last impalpable ethic purpose from the artist (most likely unconscious to himself) which I am always looking for.' When judging work, attend to subtle ethical resonances that may not be explicit but shape the work's moral effect.
